title: Marco Polo on the Silk Road
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR reaching area (100,52)-(116,68); count 1, player 1, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "VC Victory"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "Defeat Marco Dead"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 1, player 1, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "Defeat Caravan Lost"]
issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero — an 11th-century Norman duke standing in for a 13th-century Venetian teenager; a renamed generic villager/trade cart/militia would have been the correct abstraction, so this is avoidable cross-culture, cross-century casting.
Niccolo Polo is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian warlord — again a wrong-culture, wrong-era hero model where a renamed generic unit was available.
GENGHIS_KHAN is placed (in GAIA) to stand for Kublai Khan at Shangdu; right culture but the wrong Khan, dead 44 years before the scenario's arrival date.

Both players' civilizations are left RANDOM, so architecture for the Venetian caravan, the bandit camp and Shangdu is undefined — no Chinese or Central Asian architecture set is guaranteed, and Shangdu itself is rendered only as a Castle plus two Keeps.

The escort is composed of KNIGHTs and CROSSBOWMEN — a European men-at-arms escort rather than the hired local guides and guards a Venetian merchant caravan would have used across Persia and the Pamir.
The bandit force is entirely mounted (cavalry archers, light cavalry, scouts) plus an ARCHERY_RANGE, giving raiders a permanent military production building rather than a camp.
The 'Defeat Caravan Lost' condition counts player 1 objects across the whole 120x120 map rather than the pack animals specifically, so its parameters do not actually track the sheep it claims to.
strengths: Route staging is historically ordered and correctly named: Persian oasis, the Pamir 'Roof of the World', the Taklamakan wastes, then Shangdu.
Dates and details in the narration are accurate — departure 1271, Marco aged seventeen, arrival after roughly three years, and seventeen years of service to Kublai.
Yurts (eight of them) for the steppe raider camp and tents/pavilion for the caravan are the best available engine props for Central Asian encampments.
Sheep used as the caravan's pack animals is a sensible engine abstraction, and their loss is wired to a defeat condition.
Victory is an escort-to-place condition (Marco reaching the Shangdu area) with defeat on Marco's death — exactly the goal the history poses, not a combat objective.
justification: The scenario's structure is genuinely faithful: victory is bringing the Polo figure to the Shangdu area with at least one pack animal surviving, defeat is Marco's death or the loss of the caravan, and the narrated stages (Persia, Pamir, Taklamakan, Shangdu) match the sources with correct dates. The casting, however, is badly avoidable: Marco is a WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero and Niccolo an EL_CID hero, two 11th-century Western European warlords, when renamed generic units would have been correct, while Kublai is represented by his long-dead grandfather Genghis Khan. Both civilizations are left RANDOM, so the architecture of the caravan, the bandit camp and Shangdu itself (a Castle and two Keeps) is undefined for the period and region.

issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero — an 11th-century Norman duke, wrong culture and wrong century for a 13th-century Venetian merchant. A renamed generic unit (villager, trade cart driver, even a merchant-style unit) was available and would have been correct.
Niccolo Polo is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian warlord — again an unrelated culture and era for a Venetian trader.

GENGHIS_KHAN is placed (as GAIA) while the narration and victory text name Kublai Khan; Genghis died in 1227, 44 years before the journey depicted. Right culture, wrong person, and an avoidable anachronism given the text explicitly names Kublai.

Both active players are assigned civilization RANDOM, so the Polos' escort and the steppe bandits may render with any architecture set — Mongols/Persians/Saracens/Chinese were all available and appropriate.

The Venetian escort is composed of KNIGHT x3 and CROSSBOWMAN x2 under Latin-European heroes — a mounted knightly retinue is not what a merchant caravan hired across Persia and the Tarim; camels, trade carts, or light cavalry/skirmishers would have been closer.
TREE_PALM_FOREST x20 is used across the whole route; palms suit a Persian oasis but not the Pamir passes or the Taklamakan margins.
Pack animals are SHEEP; the engine offers Trade Carts and Camels, which would have represented a goods-bearing Silk Road caravan far better than a flock.
GAIA CASTLE + KEEP x2 for Shangdu gives the Khan's summer palace European fortification rather than any of the East Asian building sets available.
strengths: Player 2's raider camp is built from YURT_A-D and an archery range with CAVALRY_ARCHER, LIGHT_CAVALRY and SCOUT_CAVALRY — an entirely appropriate depiction of mounted steppe bandits preying on caravans.
The route is staged in the correct historical order: Persian oasis, bandit ambush in the dunes, the Pamir 'Roof of the World', then approach to Shangdu.

Victory is keyed to escorting the Marco Polo unit into the Shangdu area with at least one pack animal surviving — an escort/caravan-survival goal, not a generic annihilation, and it matches what the journey actually required.
Defeat on Marco's death and on the loss of the pack animals encodes the two real risks the caravan faced.
Narration is factually sound: 1271 departure, Marco aged seventeen, roughly three thousand miles, three years of travel, seventeen years in Kublai's service, Shangdu as the summer court.
Cliffs, rock formations and palisade fragments give the Pamir passage a plausible narrow-trail feel within the engine's means.
justification: The scenario's structure is genuinely good — a staged west-to-east escort with an oasis, two bandit ambushes, the Pamir crossing, and a victory condition that fires when Marco reaches Shangdu with a pack animal alive, which is precisely the historical goal. But the casting is badly avoidable: Marco Polo is a WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero and Niccolo an EL_CID, two 11th-century figures from unrelated cultures, when renamed generic units were available, and GENGHIS_KHAN stands in for the Kublai Khan the text explicitly names. Both players are left on RANDOM civilization, so the yurt camp and tent caravan — the setting's best details — sit alongside a European CASTLE and KEEP for Shangdu and palm forest across the Pamir. The written narration is accurate and would teach a player something true, but the placed content repeatedly contradicts it.

title: The Battle of Hastings
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 2) [path "[VC] Victory - Harold Slain"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "[Defeat] William Slain"]
  - TIMER + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on 1800s elapsed; count 1, player 2, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "[Defeat] Nightfall"]
issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so Norman and Anglo-Saxon architecture and unit bonuses are left to chance — the engine offers Franks/Britons (or Vikings/Celts) as obvious, avoidable choices for 1066 Normandy and England.

2,560 TREE_OAK on a 120x120 map turns Senlac Hill into dense forest; Hastings was fought on an open ridge above a shallow valley, and heavy woods also make the scripted downhill pursuit/feigned-retreat manoeuvre geographically implausible.

Harold Godwinson is represented by a KING unit — a non-combatant with no attack — rather than a renamed CHAMPION or a Teutonic/Frankish infantry hero; the historical Harold fought and died in the shield wall.

Player 2 receives 10 SKIRMISHERS; Anglo-Saxon missile troops were negligible at Hastings, and the engine's spearmen/champions alone would have represented the housecarl-and-fyrd shield wall more faithfully.
The 'Norman Reinforcements' trigger inventing 'fresh Norman riders arrive from the coast' is not attested; no reinforcements reached William during the battle — his whole force was already engaged.

Gold mines, stone mines, forage bushes and a full economic building set (Town Center, Blacksmith, Stable, Archery Range, Monastery) for both sides imply a settled base-building contest rather than a single-day pitched battle between an invasion camp and a marching army.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct, era-appropriate hero for the Norman side — the engine's own 1066 figure, not an anachronistic substitute.

Force composition matches the sources: Normans get a combined arms mix of KNIGHT (cavalry), ARCHER and SPEARMAN, while the Saxons get only foot troops (CHAMPION housecarls with axes, SPEARMAN fyrd) and no cavalry at all.
The Saxon side is numerically superior in infantry (40 foot vs 20 Norman foot), reflecting the shield wall's defensive mass on the height.

The feigned-retreat sequence is scripted properly: a hint trigger, an OBJECTS_IN_AREA 'Saxon Pursuit' that PATROLs defenders downhill, then 'Ambush Springs' killing the isolated pursuers — the battle's actual tactical turning point.

Victory fires on the death of Harold (path '[VC] Victory - Harold Slain'), the specific person the outcome of Hastings turned on, and defeat on William's death, which matches the near-collapse when rumours of his death spread.
The nightfall defeat timer encodes the real constraint: William had to break the wall before dusk or the invasion failed.
Dating and place are exact — 'October 14th, 1066... Senlac Hill' — and Harold's and William's dialogue reflects attested tactical problems (shield wall unbreakable by frontal charge).
justification: The scenario gets the human and tactical core right: William the Conqueror leads a combined knight-archer-spearman force against an all-infantry Saxon wall, the feigned retreat and ambush are actually scripted as triggers rather than merely narrated, and victory/defeat turn on Harold's death, William's death, and a nightfall deadline — precisely the stakes of 14 October 1066. The setting is the weak point: both civilizations are left RANDOM, so the architecture and bonuses may be anything from Aztec to Chinese, and 2,560 oak trees bury the open ridge of Senlac Hill in forest that would obstruct the very downhill pursuit the design depends on. Lesser avoidable errors are casting Harold as a defenceless KING rather than a renamed champion, giving the Saxons skirmishers they did not field, and inventing seaborne Norman reinforcements that never arrived.

issues_found: Both players' civilizations are left RANDOM, so Norman and Anglo-Saxon architecture sets, unit bonuses and even unit availability are arbitrary — the engine offers Franks/Britons (or Celts/Teutons) as obvious, defensible assignments, so this is avoidable.

2,560 oak trees on a 120x120 map turns Senlac Hill into dense forest; Hastings was fought over an open ridge with a slope the cavalry had to climb, and the Andredsweald lay behind the Saxon line, not across the field.

Full economic/military base furniture on the battlefield (TOWN_CENTER, BLACKSMITH, STABLE, ARCHERY_RANGE, MONASTERY for both sides) is out of place for a single-day encounter battle; only the PAVILION tents read as camp.
The 'Norman Reinforcements' trigger ('Fresh Norman riders arrive from the coast') is invented — William committed his whole host at Hastings and received no reinforcement during the battle.
Player 2 fields 10 SKIRMISHERS; Anglo-Saxon missile troops at Hastings were negligible, and the sources emphasise the Norman archery advantage.

Force ratio is inverted in scale: 31 Norman units against 51 Saxon, whereas the armies were roughly comparable in size (the Normans' edge lay in cavalry and archers, which the composition does capture).
Neither the rumour of William's death nor his raising of his helm to rally the host — the battle's genuine crisis point — appears among the 13 triggers.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR, the engine's correct hero for the Norman commander, leads Player 1.
Harold is represented by a renamed generic KING unit, and the victory trigger path ('Victory - Harold Slain') confirms it stands for him rather than being a stray unit hunt.
Force composition captures the decisive asymmetry: Normans get KNIGHTS and ARCHERS, the Saxons get no cavalry at all and rely on CHAMPIONS (housecarls with axes) and SPEARMEN as a shield wall.

The feigned-retreat sequence is modelled mechanically, not just narrated: a hint trigger, a 'Saxon Pursuit' trigger that PATROLs Saxon units downhill, and an 'Ambush Springs' trigger that kills the isolated pursuers.

Victory turns specifically on slaying Harold; defeat on William's death or on failing to break the wall by nightfall (1800s), gated on Saxon units surviving in the map area — exactly the three outcomes the day actually offered.
Date and place are stated correctly (14 October 1066, near Hastings, Senlac Hill) and the closing narration correctly ties Harold's fall to the collapse of the Saxon line.
justification: The combatant side is largely right: the engine's own William the Conqueror leads a cavalry-and-archer force against a cavalry-less Saxon body of Champions and Spearmen standing for the housecarl shield wall, with Harold cast as a renamed KING confirmed by the victory trigger path. The encoded goal is precisely historical — kill Harold, lose if William falls or if the wall still stands at nightfall — which is the exact trilemma of 14 October 1066. Setting is the weak point: both civilizations are left RANDOM despite Franks and Britons being available, and 2,560 oak trees plus Town Centres, blacksmiths and stables bury the open ridge of Senlac Hill under forest and base furniture. Events reproduce the feigned retreat and ambush mechanically rather than only in text, but invent coastal reinforcements and omit the crisis when William was rumoured dead.

Frankish (Norman knights) and Briton/Celtic (Saxon infantry/archers) were available and avoidable error.

Harold is represented by the engine's KING unit rather than a renamed generic infantry hero; the King is a non-combat courier-type unit, whereas Harold fought on foot in the shield wall with his housecarls, and the victory hinges on killing a unit that cannot fight.
2,560 oak trees blanket a 120x120 map: Senlac ridge was an open downland slope, and this much forest contradicts the open-field cavalry/archer battle the brief and dialogue describe.

Economic/settlement furniture placed for a single-day set battle — Town Centers for both sides, Blacksmith, Monastery, Archery Range, Stable, gold and stone mines, sheep and deer — none of which existed on the Hastings battlefield.
"Fresh Norman riders arrive from the coast to bolster the assault" is invented; no reinforcement column reached William during the battle — his entire force was already engaged.
Saxon SKIRMISHER x10 overstates Anglo-Saxon missile capability; the sources note Harold's army was notably short of archers.
Force totals favour the defender 51 to 31 with no Norman cavalry preponderance beyond 10 Knights, understating the roughly equal armies and the Norman mounted arm's decisive weight.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct engine hero for the correct person, century and campaign.
The Anglo-Saxon roster is entirely dismounted — Champions (housecarls with axes) and massed Spearmen for the shield wall — correctly denying Harold any cavalry.

The feigned-retreat sequence is modelled mechanically, not just narrated: an OBJECTS_IN_AREA trigger springs a Saxon PATROL downhill and a KILL_OBJECT ambush destroys the pursuers, which is the actual tactical turning point of the battle.
Victory fires on the death of the unit standing for Harold under the path "Victory - Harold Slain", exactly the event that decided the day.

Defeat on William's death mirrors the real crisis when a rumour of William's fall nearly routed the Norman line, and the 1800-second nightfall defeat encodes the genuine constraint that William had to break the wall before dark or lose his campaign.
The date (October 14th, 1066), the place name Senlac Hill, and Harold Godwinson's claim to the crown are all stated correctly.
justification: The scenario gets the tactical substance of Hastings right: an all-infantry Saxon shield wall of Champions and Spearmen on a ridge, a Norman force of Knights and Archers under the correct William hero, and a scripted feigned retreat that lures pursuers into a scripted ambush. Its victory and defeat conditions are the historical ones — kill Harold, do not lose William, and do it before the 30-minute nightfall deadline. The setting is the weak point: both civilizations are left RANDOM despite Frankish and Briton being obvious choices, 2,560 trees smother what should be open downland, and Town Centres, a Blacksmith, mines and livestock clutter a one-day battlefield. Invented Norman reinforcements from the coast and Harold cast as the non-combatant KING unit are the remaining avoidable errors.

objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on SALADIN (player 2) [path "[VC] Abd al-Rahman Slain"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 3, player 3, area (40,92)-(80,115) [path "[VC] Umayyad Withdrawal"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "[Loss] Charles Martel Killed"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 10, player 2, area (40,15)-(80,35) [path "[Loss] Shield Wall Overrun"]
issues_found: Charles Martel is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero — a Norman duke of 1066, over three centuries after Tours; a renamed generic Frankish champion/paladin was available and would have been correct.
Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is represented by SALADIN, a 12th-century Ayyubid sultan of an entirely different dynasty and era; again avoidable via a renamed Saracen cavalry unit.
Duke Odo of Aquitaine is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian — wrong culture, wrong polity, wrong century.
Both active players are set to civilization RANDOM, so architecture, unit skins and bonuses are undefined; Franks vs Saracens were obvious and available assignments.

Player 2's Umayyad force includes 6 KNIGHTS (Frankish/European heavy cavalry look) alongside camels and cavalry archers, blurring the visual distinction between the two armies — Saracen mamluks/light cavalry would have read better.
Frankish force is tiny (20 infantry) against a similarly tiny mounted force; the sources describe a large Frankish infantry mass, and 4,758 objects are almost entirely trees rather than troops.
Player 2 holds a lone VILLAGER_MALE and only tents/pavilions for the 'camp' that Odo is supposed to burn — the plunder-laden Umayyad baggage camp central to the narrative is barely represented.
strengths: Terrain is a genuinely wooded ridge (4,640 oak trees) matching the forested high ground between Tours and Poitiers, with the Franks deployed on the defensive.
Frankish force is correctly infantry-only (militia line, spearmen, pikemen) versus an all-mounted Umayyad force — the tactical asymmetry of the battle.

Scripted sequence reproduces the historical shape: successive cavalry charges, the Aquitanian/Frankish raid on the enemy camp, the death of Abd al-Rahman, and the Umayyad withdrawal under cover of night.

Victory conditions are keyed to the historically decisive events — slaying Abd al-Rahman (path names him explicitly, so the SALADIN target is a renamed commander, not a unit hunt) or getting Odo's men into the enemy camp area — and defeat to Martel's death or the shield wall being overrun.
In-game text quotes the Mozarabic Chronicle's 'like a wall, immovable as a block of ice' and dates the battle correctly to October 732.
justification: The scenario's structure is strong: forested defensive ridge, infantry-versus-cavalry asymmetry, scripted charges, the camp raid, and victory conditions tied to Abd al-Rahman's death or the flank force reaching the camp, with defeat on Martel's fall or the wall being overrun — precisely what the history posed. Its failures are in casting and configuration: all three commanders are represented by heroes from the wrong century and, in El Cid's and William's cases, the wrong polity, when renamed generic units were an available and correct solution, and both players are left on RANDOM civilization so architecture and unit appearance are undefined. The narration itself is accurate and even quotes the Mozarabic Chronicle correctly, so a playthrough teaches the right battle despite Saladin and William standing in the field.

Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is represented by SALADIN, a 12th-century Kurdish Ayyubid sultan of an entirely different dynasty and era from an 8th-century Umayyad governor of al-Andalus
Duke Odo of Aquitaine is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian — wrong century and wrong polity

Odo's contingent is issued SCOUT_CAVALRY and KNIGHT but the Aquitanians who raided the camp were part of Martel's coalition rather than a separate third civilization with its own camp

Umayyad force is entirely mounted (Camel Rider, Cavalry Archer, Knight) with a single villager for the camp, matching the sources' cavalry host

The casting, however, is badly anachronistic and avoidable: William the Conqueror plays Charles Martel, Saladin plays an 8th-century Umayyad governor, and El Cid plays Duke Odo, when renamed generic units were available. Leaving both active players on RANDOM civilization also strips the scenario of any assigned Frankish or Andalusi architecture, undercutting an otherwise appropriate forested map.

issues_found: Charles Martel is represented by WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR, a Norman duke of the 1060s — over three centuries after Tours; a renamed generic infantry hero or Militia/Champion would have been correct.
Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is represented by SALADIN, a 12th-century Kurdish Ayyubid sultan — wrong dynasty, wrong culture, and 450 years late for an Umayyad emir of al-Andalus.
Duke Odo of Aquitaine is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian; even confining oneself to shipped heroes this is an unrelated era and polity.

Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so architecture and unit sets are left to chance; Franks (P1) and Saracens/Berbers (P2) were both available and would have fixed the building styles.
Player 3 (Odo's Aquitanians) has no civilization entry at all, leaving the allied contingent's appearance undefined.
PIKEMAN among the Frankish line is a late-medieval unit; the Militia/Spearman line alone would have carried the shield-wall abstraction without the anachronism.
Force scale is very small (about 20 Franks, 21 Umayyads) for an engagement of tens of thousands, though this is partly a medium constraint.
strengths: Correct date and place stated (October 732, between Tours and Poitiers) with no invented events.
Terrain is a heavily wooded ridge (4,640 oaks) matching the sources' wooded high ground, with the Franks defending uphill and the Umayyad camp to the south.

Force character is right: Frankish foot (Militia/Man-at-Arms/Champion/Spearman/Pikeman) versus an all-mounted Umayyad force of Camel Riders, Cavalry Archers and Knights, plus a small Umayyad camp with tents and pavilions to be raided.
The turning points are reproduced in order: repeated cavalry charges against a holding line, the Aquitanian strike on the baggage camp, and the Umayyad withdrawal under cover of night.

Victory conditions are keyed to the historical outcomes — the death of the emir (trigger path names Abd al-Rahman) or the Aquitanians reaching the enemy camp — with defeat on Martel's death or the line being overrun, exactly the loss the Franks faced.

justification: The scenario's geography, force composition, event sequence and win/loss logic are unusually faithful: a wooded ridge, infantry-versus-cavalry, repeated charges, Odo's raid on the baggage camp, and victory keyed either to slaying the emir or to the Aquitanians reaching the camp, with defeat on Martel's death or the wall being overrun. The damage is all in casting and configuration: all three commanders are heroes from the wrong centuries and cultures (William the Conqueror as Charles Martel, Saladin as Abd al-Rahman, El Cid as Odo) when renamed generics were available, and both active players are left on RANDOM civilization so the Frankish and Umayyad architecture is arbitrary. The engine ships no Mehmed hero, but a renamed generic unit (as was done for Constantine with KING) was available, so this substitution is avoidable and doubly wrong in both culture and era.

TREE_PALM_FOREST x10 and CLIFF objects are wrong flora and terrain for Thracian Constantinople.

SHEEP x12, GOLD_MINE x10, STONE_MINE x8 and FORAGE_BUSH x8 give the besieged city an open economy it did not have; a starving blockaded capital should be resource-poor.
strengths: Constantine XI is correctly represented by a KING unit and his death is a defeat condition — historically exact, since the Emperor fell at the walls and the defence collapsed with him.

The Ottoman siege train is right: BOMBARD_CANNON x3 and MANGONEL x2 in a SIEGE_WORKSHOP-backed force reflect Orban's great guns, and the [Event] The Wall is Breached trigger KILLs a wall segment under cannon fire, reproducing the actual mechanism of the city's fall.

The escalating wave structure (probing assault, bombardment, assault through the breach, weeks of attrition, then Mehmed's general assault) tracks the real April–May 1453 sequence in the correct order.
Giovanni Giustiniani's arrival with Genoese troops is a genuine and well-chosen historical detail, delivered by a CREATE_OBJECT reinforcement trigger.
The area-based defeat trigger on the Hagia Sophia district and the MONASTERY-loss defeat correctly identify the loss the defenders actually faced, rather than a generic wipe-out.
Narration text is factually sound: eleven centuries of the city, Constantine's refusal of Mehmed's ultimatum, and the Theodosian Walls patched with rubble.
justification: The scenario gets the shape of the siege right — bombards breaching a wall via a scripted KILL_OBJECT, escalating assault waves, Giustiniani's Genoese, and defeat on the Emperor's death or the Hagia Sophia district being overrun — but it fatally miscasts the besieger by placing SALADIN, a 12th-century Ayyubid, as Mehmed II when the same renamed-generic trick used for Constantine's KING was available. Both civilizations are left RANDOM, so no Byzantine or Turkish architecture is guaranteed, palm forests and cliffs stand in for Thrace, and the Golden Horn sea walls the brief foregrounds have no water, docks, or ships at all. The objective is of the right kind — a 600-second hold with defeat on the Emperor and the Hagia Sophia — but its victory trigger perversely requires the destruction of the player's own MONASTERY, the very Hagia Sophia proxy whose loss is simultaneously coded as defeat.

Three historically distinct opponents — the Merkits, Jamukha's Jadaran, and the Naiman confederation — are collapsed into a single Player 2 whose roster never changes, so the player fights the same warband under three different names.

Tayang Khan of the Naiman is represented by the KING unit, a sceptred European monarch on foot; a renamed cavalry archer or light cavalry would have been the more plausible steppe khan.

Toghrul / Wang Khan of the Kereit is entirely absent, yet his patronage of Temujin and the 1203 war against him were the decisive step before the Naiman campaign — the narration jumps straight from Jamukha to Tayang Khan.
The alliance with Jamukha is triggered AFTER Borte's rescue; in the sources Jamukha and Toghrul supplied the army that carried out the rescue, so the causal order is inverted.
All the dialogue beats and enemy attacks fire on TIMERs rather than on player accomplishment, so the 1186-1206 arc plays out on a clock regardless of what the player does.
Only one female villager on Player 2's side stands for Borte, and nothing marks her; the BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA rescue works but relies on the player guessing which unit she is.
strengths: Temujin is cast as the engine's GENGHIS_KHAN hero — the correct person, culture and era — and his death is the defeat condition, matching the fact that the confederation depended wholly on him.
Force composition is right for the steppe: 11 and 8 cavalry archers plus 10 light cavalry, with almost no infantry and only two guard towers.
Nomadic settlement is dressed with YURT_A through YURT_D on both sides plus bonfires, sheep, deer and rock formations, which reads as an encampment on open grassland rather than a walled town.

The narrative sequence — Merkit abduction of Borte, alliance with Jamukha, Jamukha's breaking of the blood-oath, the shattering of the Naiman, the 1206 kurultai — follows the actual arc, and the dates 1186 and 1206 are both correct.

Victory keyed to destroying Player 2's KING, which the [Obj2] trigger identifies as Tayang Khan, ties the win to the specific rival whose death broke the last confederation opposing Temujin, rather than to wiping out the map.
The kurultai and the title 'Ruler of All Peoples' are stated correctly in the closing text.
justification: The scenario gets the protagonist exactly right — the GENGHIS_KHAN hero as Temujin, an all-mounted warband of cavalry archers and light cavalry, and yurt encampments on open steppe — and its narrative beats (Borte's abduction, the Jamukha alliance and betrayal, Tayang Khan's fall, the 1206 kurultai) follow the sources in the right order with correct dates. The main failures are structural rather than textual: both civilizations are left RANDOM despite the Mongols being available, three separate enemies (Merkit, Jadaran, Naiman) are all worn by one unchanging Player 2, Jamukha is never placed as a unit at all, and Toghrul of the Kereit — the indispensable patron and the 1203 war — is missing entirely. Three escalating assaults followed by 'October rains flood the Ottoman trenches' and the 14 October withdrawal reproduce the correct sequence and outcome, with accurate dating.
Roman Ruins on the map is a quiet nod to Vindobona beneath Vienna.
Victory is a hold-until-relieved timer with the Town Center/commander as defeat conditions — the correct form for a siege the defenders only had to outlast.
justification: The scenario gets the shape of 1529 right — Suleiman and Salm as named Kings, a walled city against an external tent camp, a scripted mine detonation and breach, three assaults, and withdrawal on 14 October — and encodes the correct goal: survive a timer while keeping the Town Center and commander alive. It is undercut by two avoidable choices: both civilizations are left RANDOM, so nothing about the architecture is pinned to Habsburg Vienna or the Ottomans, and the arquebusiers and Janissaries the text names are represented by nobody, even though Hand Cannoneers exist in the engine. The Ottoman force is also implausibly cavalry-heavy and carries a Bombard Cannon the real besiegers largely lacked. Narration remains accurate and well-dated, so a playthrough still teaches the right story despite the roster contradicting its own dialogue.

title: The Battle of Hastings
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS

issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so Norman and Anglo-Saxon architecture and unit bonuses are left to chance (Franks/Britons were the obvious, available choices).

Player 2 (the Saxons) is given 44 STONE_WALL segments, a GATE_NORTH_TO_SOUTH and 4 GUARD_TOWERs. Harold's army fought a field battle behind a shield wall of men on an open ridge; there were no fortifications at Senlac, and the walls flatly contradict the scenario's own narration about breaking a shield wall.

4,174 TREE_OAK objects dominate a 120x120 map; the Hastings battlefield was an open slope with marshy ground below the ridge, not dense forest, and heavy woods make cavalry envelopment and the feigned-retreat pursuit unrepresentable.

Both sides own TOWN_CENTER, STABLE, ARCHERY_RANGE, BLACKSMITH and MONASTERY - base furniture for a one-day pitched battle where neither army had a settlement; a Norman TOWN_CENTER loss is even wired as a defeat condition, an event with no historical counterpart.
The Saxon force includes 16 SKIRMISHERs; Harold's army was notably short of missile troops, and this over-arms the shield wall with skirmishers while the Normans get only 10 archers.
Secondary victory 'VC2' awards the win merely for having one unit alive anywhere on the map at 600 seconds, so a passive player can win without ever engaging the shield wall.

Dialogue line 'The Duke has fallen! Normandy's cause dies with him!' fires on William's death - a counterfactual outcome presented without flagging that William in fact survived (only rumours of his death circulated).
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR, the engine's own correct hero for this exact battle, commands the Norman side.
Norman roster is a genuine combined-arms force - 21 KNIGHT, 12 MAN_AT_ARMS, 10 ARCHER - matching the cavalry/infantry/archer combination the sources describe.

Saxon roster of 25 CHAMPION (housecarls) plus 20 SPEARMAN (fyrd levies) is a sound engine abstraction of the shield wall, and the KING unit is a reasonable renamed stand-in for Harold, for whom the engine ships no hero.
Primary victory condition fires on the death of the KING (Harold), the actual decisive event of 14 October 1066, and defeat on William's loss.
Narration is dated correctly (October 14th, 1066), names Senlac Hill, the marshy ground below the ridge, housecarls and fyrd, the feigned retreats, and the dusk deadline.
justification: The combatant casting is strong: William the Conqueror himself leads Normans of knights, men-at-arms and archers against housecarl champions and fyrd spearmen under a King standing in for Harold, and victory is keyed precisely to Harold's death - the historical turning point. The setting, however, is the weak link: both civilizations are left RANDOM, the Saxons are walled in with 44 stone wall segments, a gate and four guard towers despite the narration's insistence on an open shield wall, and 4,174 oaks bury a battlefield that was open slope and marsh. A redundant 600-second 'survive with one unit anywhere' victory also lets the player win without ever assaulting the hill, and Norman town-centre loss as defeat is an invented condition.

Player 2 fields 20 CAVALRY_ARCHER, an over-weighting of horse archery for an Andalusian Umayyad force whose strength was lance-and-sword heavy cavalry.
The 600-second alternate victory is a rather thin representation of a day-long (reportedly multi-day) stand.
Defeat on the loss of Player 1's TOWN_CENTER is a generic base-loss condition; the Franks at Tours held a battlefield ridge, not a town.
strengths: Frankish force is infantry-heavy (20 spearmen, 10 militia, 4 men-at-arms, 8 archers) against an all-mounted Umayyad roster (knights, camel riders, cavalry archers) — exactly the infantry-square-versus-cavalry dynamic the sources describe.

5,883 oak trees create the genuinely wooded, broken high ground that historians credit for blunting the Umayyad charges, and dialogue ties the terrain to the tactic ('our charge has broken against the trees').
The third player as Odo of Aquitaine, rallied by a BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA trigger to strike the enemy camp, reproduces the camp-raid that reportedly precipitated the Umayyad withdrawal.
Victory keyed to the death of the enemy commander matches the historical outcome — Abd al-Rahman was killed and his army dispersed.
Narration is correctly dated to October 732 and names Tours, Poitiers, Charles Martel, Abd al-Rahman and Odo without inventing events.
justification: The tactical skeleton is right: a static, infantry-only Frankish line in dense woodland absorbing an all-cavalry Umayyad army, with an Aquitanian third party that can be rallied against the enemy camp, and victory that fires when the enemy commander is slain — precisely how the battle was decided. The casting, however, is triply anachronistic in ways the engine did not force: William the Conqueror plays Charles Martel, Saladin plays Abd al-Rahman, and El Cid plays Duke Odo, when renamed generic units were the correct solution for figures the game ships no hero for. Setting is further undercut by leaving both civilizations RANDOM and by giving the Umayyad raiding camp a stone castle with walls, gate and guard towers. The in-game text itself is accurate and would teach the player the correct names, date and tactical lesson.

issues_found: Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the architecture set, unit skins and bonuses of the French escort and the Anglo-Burgundian garrison of Troyes are undetermined at load time; Franks and Britons were both available and would have fixed this.

The Troyes/Chalons garrison is armed with Crossbowmen and Pikemen; the engine ships the Longbowman, the obvious and available representation of an English garrison of 1429, and the Anglo-Burgundian character of the Champagne garrisons is not signalled at all.

The brief promises garrisons that 'can be fought or persuaded to surrender' — historically Troyes capitulated after negotiation and a show of assault preparations, and Chalons simply opened its gates — but the only encoded interaction is the 'Gate Breached' destroy trigger. There is no surrender or diplomacy path.

The 'Ambush at the river crossing' near Chalons and the raider-chief side quest that recruits French villager pikemen are inventions; the march from Gien to Reims was notable precisely for its near-absence of fighting.
Victory fires on JOAN_OF_ARC reaching Reims, not on the KING (Dauphin Charles), directly contradicting the brief's own statement that 'Victory requires the Dauphin reaching Reims cathedral alive'.

None of the captains who actually accompanied the march (Alencon, Dunois, La Hire, La Tremoille) are represented even as renamed generics; the royal army of roughly twelve thousand is reduced to five Knights and five Crossbowmen.

Reims cathedral is a MONASTERY and Troyes is a single CASTLE with sixteen wall segments and two guard towers — acceptable abstraction, but the Roman Ruins and Pavilion/Tent decorations are the only civic dressing on a 120x120 map otherwise filled with 2,880 oak trees.
strengths: Joan of Arc is the engine's actual Joan of Arc hero, not a substituted figure from another century, and the Dauphin is a KING unit — the correct available stand-in for an uncrowned Charles VII.
Defeat on the death of the KING encodes the real stake: without Charles there is no coronation, exactly as the brief states.
The narrative sequence is correct and correctly dated: June 1429, after Orleans, through English-held Champagne, past Troyes and Chalons, ending with the coronation as Charles VII.
The staged BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA dialogue beacons plus the two timed 'Pursuit Wave' triggers model a column under march pressure rather than a static battle, which suits an escort operation.
Roman Ruins are a defensible touch for Reims, which retains the Roman Porte de Mars.
justification: The scenario gets the principals right — the engine's own Joan of Arc hero escorting a KING as the uncrowned Dauphin, with defeat on his death — and its text places the march accurately in June 1429 between Orleans and the coronation. It is undermined by leaving both active players on RANDOM civilization, so neither the French column nor the Champagne garrison has a determined architecture or roster, and by arming the English with Crossbowmen when Longbowmen were available. The events drift where it matters most: Troyes and Chalons can only be stormed, never persuaded to surrender as they historically were, and an invented river ambush and raider-chief quest fill the space. The victory condition is of the right kind and keyed to the right place, but it fires on Joan reaching Reims rather than on the Dauphin, contradicting the brief's own stated goal.

The 'Forest Ambush' trigger (five PATROL actions on English scouts) is an invention with no basis in the sources for the June–July 1429 march.

Only one GAIA MONASTERY stands in for Reims cathedral; no Wonder or larger sacred structure was used to mark the coronation site, so the 'twin towers of Reims cathedral' text is unsupported by placed content.
strengths: JOAN_OF_ARC is the engine's correct named hero for the protagonist and is placed on the escorting side.
The Dauphin is represented by a KING object — the right choice for an uncrowned monarch whose loss ends the campaign, and it makes both victory and defeat conditions key on him.
Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on the KING at the Reims cathedral area, exactly the historical goal (reaching Reims for coronation), not an enemy-elimination default.
Defeat on the KING's death matches the actual stake: without Charles there is no coronation and no Valois cause.

Both Troyes and Châlons have dual resolution paths — 'Falls in Battle' (DESTROY_OBJECT) and 'Surrenders' (BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA) with CHANGE_OWNERSHIP — faithfully modelling that both towns actually capitulated rather than being stormed.
Sequential geography (Troyes approach, then Châlons approach, then Reims arrival) reproduces the correct west-to-east order of the march.
Heavy oak forest, deer and sheep are plausible for the Champagne countryside of the route.
justification: The scenario's skeleton is unusually faithful: the King object stands for the Dauphin, victory fires on bringing him to the Reims cathedral area, defeat on his death, and each garrison can be either destroyed or persuaded to surrender — precisely what happened at Troyes and Châlons in July 1429. That accuracy is undercut by casting: the English garrison commanders are El Cid and William the Conqueror, one from eleventh-century Castile and one from 1066 Normandy, when a renamed generic unit was available and correct, and no longbowmen appear at all. Both civilizations are left RANDOM, so the architecture and tech of Troyes, Châlons and the escort are undetermined, and the invented forest ambush plus an 11-man escort standing for a 12,000-strong royal army further thin the representation. The narration itself is honest and well dated, so a playthrough still teaches the right campaign.

justification: The scenario's siege architecture, countermining sortie, three gate assaults and rain-driven Ottoman withdrawal capture the shape of September-October 1529, but the casting is badly wrong in avoidable ways: Saladin plays Suleiman and Frederick Barbarossa plays Niklas Graf Salm, both centuries and (in Saladin's case) cultures displaced, when renamed generics were available. Both civilizations are left RANDOM, so nothing about the architecture or unit lines is anchored to Habsburg Vienna or the Porte, and camel riders and defender bombard cannons compound the confusion. Most damagingly, victory fires on the death of the enemy sultan - an event that did not happen and inverts a siege the defenders had only to outlast - and the closing text tells the player Suleiman's banner fell before Vienna.

Three timed assault waves with PATROL effects reproduce the historical pattern of successive storms against the Carinthian Gate breach.

No structure represents Shangdu (Xanadu): the victory area (60,30)-(70,50) contains no palace, castle, wonder or town centre — the destination the whole scenario is named for is empty ground.

The narrative invents hostility from the Khan's own men ('Ambush! The riders of the Khan were waiting in the rocks!', 'A Mongol camp guards the mountain pass ahead!'). Historically the Polos travelled with Kublai's golden tablet and were escorted and welcomed, not pursued and ambushed by Mongol riders.
The three-and-a-half-year journey via Acre, Hormuz, the Pamirs and the Gobi is compressed into a single generic desert/palm-forest map with no distinguishable stages beyond text triggers.
strengths: The victory condition encodes exactly the historical goal: bring the protagonist alive to the destination at Shangdu, with defeat on his death rather than on destroying an enemy force.
Player 2's camp of YURT_A-D with a palisade, gate and guard tower is a plausible steppe encampment for the route through Central Asia.
Terrain and gaia decoration (palm forest, rock formations, cliffs, oasis forage, gold and stone mines, bonfire, tents and a market as a trade post) evoke a desert caravan route reasonably well.
Text correctly names the date 1271, Niccolo, Kublai Khan and the summer palace at Shangdu, and the waypoint triggers give the journey a departure-midpoint-arrival structure.
The 'Find Allies / Allies Join' quest (slay the bandit chief, gain the caravan guards via CHANGE_OWNERSHIP) is a period-plausible caravan-escort mechanic.
justification: The encoded objective is genuinely the historical one — escort the protagonist to Shangdu, lose if he dies — and the desert/yurt setting is atmospherically reasonable, but the casting is badly wrong: Marco Polo is played by Richard the Lionheart, a Plantagenet crusader from a different culture and century, when a renamed generic unit was available; Niccolo is dialogue-only; and the caravan's pack animals, the very thing the brief says must survive, were never placed. Both players are left on RANDOM civilization and no building stands at the Shangdu victory area. The narration further invents Kublai's own riders ambushing the Polos, inverting the paiza-protected passage the sources describe.

4,800 oak trees on a 120x120 map turns the open downland of Senlac/Caldbec Hill into dense forest; the battle was fought on bare open slopes with marsh at the foot.

The Anglo-Saxon side is given a CASTLE, 29 STONE_WALL segments, 2 gates and 4 GUARD_TOWERs. Harold's army held an unfortified ridge; there was no fortification at Hastings, and the 'Raze the Saxon Castle' objective invents a structure outright.

The 900-second 'nightfall' victory lets the player win by merely surviving, whereas historically dusk came only after the shield wall had broken and Harold was dead.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct hero for the correct battle and century, placed on the correct side.
Harold is represented by a KING unit — a unique, singled-out target rather than a line unit — and victory keys on his death, exactly as the battle was decided.
The Saxon roster is entirely infantry (4 CHAMPION as huscarls, 15 MAN_AT_ARMS, 15 SPEARMAN), a faithful abstraction of a dismounted shield wall.
The Norman roster is genuinely combined-arms (archers, man-at-arms, knights), matching the archer-infantry-cavalry sequence described in the sources.
Text correctly dates the battle to 14 October 1066, names Senlac Hill, and distinguishes huscarls at the centre from fyrd on the flanks.
Defeat on William's death correctly encodes the fact that the invasion hinged on the duke's survival (cf. the rumour of his death nearly routing his army).
justification: The combatants are handled well — the correct named Norman hero, a KING standing in for Harold with victory keyed to slaying him, and an all-infantry Saxon shield wall — and the narration is accurate on date, place, and the huscarl/fyrd deployment. The setting, however, is badly compromised: both civilizations are left RANDOM despite Franks and Britons being available, 4,800 oaks bury the open downs of Senlac in forest, and the Saxons are given a Castle, guard towers and 29 wall segments plus a 'raze the castle' objective for a position that had no fortifications at all. Events keep the broad shape (archer volley, pressing the wall, Harold's fall at dusk) but the signature feigned retreat is only asserted in dialogue with no trigger implementing it, and a Norman Town Center defeat invents a Saxon strike on the beachhead.

The setting undercuts this badly — both civilizations are left RANDOM, the ridge is smothered in 4,800 trees, and the Saxons are given a Castle, 29 stone walls, gates and guard towers, which is precisely the fortification technology the Normans introduced after 1066 and the opposite of an unfortified shield wall on open ground. Player 2's army is 28 Camel Riders and 31 Cavalry Archers with no infantry, which reads as a Saracen desert host rather than an Almoravid Berber force of light horse, javelin infantry and drummers; the mass of camelry is also wildly disproportionate to El Cid's 16-man retinue.

The narrative is a generic quest template: 'raider outpost', 'Ambusher', an unnamed 'Traitor King', 'Villain Confrontation', 'Villain Speech'. None of El Cid's actual campaigns (Almenar 1082, Morella, the capture of Berenguer Ramon II at Tevar 1090, the siege of Valencia 1093-94, Cuarte 1094) appear.

Opening narration correctly dates the exile to 1081, names King Alfonso VI of Castile as the one who banished him, and correctly identifies the taifa of Zaragoza and Al-Mutamin as his paymaster.
The player's starting force (Knights, Spearmen, Archers, a small Town Center with Stable/Barracks/Archery Range) is a reasonable abstraction of a Castilian mesnada of household cavalry.

ROMAN_RUINS as a landmark is period-plausible for the Ebro frontier.
justification: The scenario gets its protagonist right, correctly names Alfonso VI, Al-Mutamin and the taifa of Zaragoza, and correctly makes El Cid's own survival the defeat condition, but the antagonist is Saladin, a figure of the wrong century and the wrong end of the Mediterranean, backed by 59 camel riders and cavalry archers rather than an Almoravid host. Both civilizations are left RANDOM, so nothing anchors the architecture to Iberia. The dialogue chain is a generic quest template of bandit outposts, ambushes and an unnamed 'Traitor King' rather than Almenar, Tevar or the siege of Valencia, and victory is the default decapitation of the enemy commander instead of the capture of Valencia the brief promises.

Civilizations are left RANDOM, the map is dressed in palm forest, and the promised Golden Horn sea walls and Ottoman fleet do not exist, while the assaults come from the north, east and south rather than the western land walls.

Events preserve the shape of the march past Troyes and Chalons but replace the historical surrenders with a storm-only gate and add an invented bandit-chief side quest.

strengths: William the Conqueror is the engine's own correct hero for the Norman commander — right person, right year.
A rename trigger converts the enemy KING into Harold Godwinson, so the victory target is the historical king rather than an anonymous unit.
The Anglo-Saxon roster contains no cavalry and only 4 archers against 20 Champions and 20 Spearmen, correctly reflecting a dismounted shield wall short of missile troops.

Victory on Harold's death and defeat on nightfall (1500s) with Harold still standing reproduce exactly the two ways the day could have ended; defeat on William's fall matches the panic caused by the rumour of his death.
Narration is factually precise: 14 October 1066, Senlac Hill, the road to London, the 'Out! Out!' Saxon cry, and Harold struck down before his own line.
justification: The scenario gets the people and the stakes right — the engine's genuine William the Conqueror hero, a renamed King Harold, an all-infantry Saxon line with almost no archers, and a trigger set whose victory is Harold's death and whose defeat is nightfall with the wall unbroken, which is precisely the historical dilemma. The setting is where it fails: both civilizations are left RANDOM, so architecture and unit appearance are arbitrary, and 4,800 trees plus ten gold mines, eight stone mines and a full Norman building set convert an open one-day battlefield into a generic forested economy map. Events are well narrated but the signature feigned retreat is only a text message rather than a modelled Saxon break in formation, and 20 knights to 10 foot inverts the Norman army's actual infantry-heavy composition.

Only 107 objects on a 120x120 map: Zaragoza, Tevar and Valencia are all represented by the single Player 2 town centre/castle complex rather than as distinct locations, so the geography of the exile is not really depicted.
strengths: The actual EL_CID hero unit is used for Rodrigo Diaz, the correct person, culture and century, and the Spanish civilization is correctly assigned to him.
The player's starting force — 1 hero, 3 men-at-arms, 2 spearmen, 3 villagers, a barracks and a town centre — accurately models a landless exile's small mounted retinue rather than a royal army.

The three-stage progression (mercenary service to Zaragoza 1081, Tevar 1090 against Berenguer Ramon II, Valencia 1094) matches the sequence and dating of the historical exile, including the correct year for Tébar and for the fall of Valencia.

Retinue growth is mechanically tied to victories (MODIFY_RESOURCE plus CREATE_OBJECT on each battle won), reproducing the historical pattern of El Cid's following swelling with each success.
justification: The scenario gets the protagonist exactly right — the engine's own El Cid hero, a genuinely small exile's retinue, and a victory condition keyed to breaking the Alcazar of Valencia in 1094 rather than to wiping out an enemy army. Its central flaw is combatant-side: every opponent from the rival taifas to Berenguer Ramon II, Count of Barcelona, is folded into one Saracen player, so the Catalan Christian army at Tevar fields camel riders and Saracen buildings when a second Spanish or Frankish player was available. The event chain (exile 1081, service to Zaragoza, Tevar 1090, Valencia 1094) is correctly ordered and dated, marred only by the invented 'raiders' opening standing in for documented fights like Almenar, and by the absence of al-Mu'tamin as an actual player.

justification: The scenario casts the correct principal (GENGHIS_KHAN as Temujin) and names Toghtoa Beki, Borte, Jamukha and Tayang Khan on placed units, with an all-cavalry roster and yurt-and-bonfire steppe camps that are entirely plausible for 1186-1206; the intrusive KNIGHT and CAVALIER on the enemy side and the compression of Merkit, Jadaran and Naiman into one TURKS player are the main avoidable faults. The event chain — Borte's rescue, the Jamukha pact, its rupture, the Naiman war, the kurultai — has the right shape, but it omits Toghrul of the Kereit entirely, inverts the order of the rescue and the alliance, and misdates Tayang Khan's death to 1206. The victory condition kills the Cavalier standing for Tayang Khan under a path naming the Naiman defeat and the kurultai, so it is keyed to the historical turning point rather than being a unit hunt, and defeat on Temujin's death is exactly the loss he faced.

strengths: JOAN_OF_ARC is the engine's own correct hero for the correct campaign and year, not a substitute

justification: The scenario gets the hardest part right: victory fires when the renamed KING (the Dauphin) enters the Reims cathedral area and defeat on his death, which is precisely the historical stake of the Loire-to-Reims march, and Joan is the engine's own correct hero rather than a substitute. Setting and force composition are sound for 1429, though the English side uses generic Archers instead of the available Briton Longbowman and none of Joan's named companions (Alencon, La Hire) appear. The main historical slips are labelling Troyes and Chalons as English rather than Burgundian-allegiance towns, omitting Auxerre, compressing the multi-day Troyes standoff into an immediate opening of the gates, and inventing two garrison sorties that never occurred.

title: The Road to Reims
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS

Victory:

Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 1) [path "[Defeat] The Dauphin Falls"]
issues_found: Troyes and Chalons were held by Anglo-Burgundian garrisons whose loyalty was primarily to Philip the Good, not purely 'English-held' as the narration and the Briton assignment assert; the Burgundian dimension that actually explains the negotiated surrenders is absent from both roster and text.

The [Ambush] Troyes Sortie and Chalons Sortie triggers invent armed sallies by garrisons that in fact never engaged the royal column; Troyes' resistance was passive (closed gates and refusal of supplies) until it capitulated on terms.

Player 2 fields Cavalier x3 and Knight x3 - mounted men-at-arms are a poor fit for small-town English/Burgundian garrison companies, which were archer- and billman-heavy; the Archer x8 and Spearman x6 already carried that load.
900 oak trees on a 120x120 map over-forests the Champagne plain, the open cereal country the royal progress actually crossed.

No representation of the negotiated element on the French side (Brother Richard, the Archbishop Regnault de Chartres, or the town deputations) that made Troyes' surrender possible - the only mechanism is a proximity trigger.
strengths: JOAN_OF_ARC is the engine's own hero for the correct figure and correct year, not a substitution.
The Dauphin is a KING object renamed via a setup CHANGE_OBJECT_NAME trigger - the correct handling for a figure the engine ships no hero for.

Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on the King at the Reims cathedral tile block, keyed to the exact person and place the history singles out; defeat is the Dauphin's death, the one loss that would have voided the coronation.
Correct sequence and outcome: Troyes first, then Chalons, both yielding without assault, then the coronation dated 17 July 1429 as King Charles VII.
Franks for the French royal party and Britons for the English garrisons is the standard and defensible mapping within the engine's catalogue, and both are explicitly assigned.
justification: The scenario casts the correct principals with the engine's actual Joan of Arc hero and a renamed KING for the Dauphin, and its victory condition - the King reaching the Reims cathedral area, with his death as defeat - is precisely the goal the 1429 progress posed, rather than a generic destroy-the-enemy default. The event sequence (Troyes yields rather than face siege, Chalons submits without a blow, coronation on 17 July) matches the sources in shape and order. Deductions are for calling the Troyes and Chalons garrisons flatly 'English' when they were Anglo-Burgundian, for the invented Troyes and Chalons sorties that no source records, and for a heavily forested map and mounted garrison troops that fit Champagne and small-town garrison companies poorly.

GAIA MONASTERY standing in for Reims Cathedral is the best the catalogue offers, but the two additional Player 2 MONASTERY buildings inside English-held towns are unexplained clutter.

Franks for the French column and Britons for the English-held towns is the natural civilization mapping.
Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on the King at the Reims cathedral area, and defeat is the King's death - exactly the historical stake of the march.
Both towns can be bypassed or persuaded rather than stormed, mirroring the bloodless submissions of Troyes and Chalons.
The coronation date given, 17 July 1429, and the title 'King Charles VII' are correct.

Setting and force composition are plausible for 1429 Champagne, with the main slip being that Troyes and Chalons are presented as English rather than Anglo-Burgundian garrisons. Events follow the real shape and the closing date of 17 July 1429 is correct, but Auxerre is omitted, Troyes yields on contact rather than after several days of standoff and assault preparations, and the two 'sortie' ambushes are invented for gameplay.

title: The Siege of Vienna
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - TIMER on 300s elapsed [path "VC - Siege Lifted"]
Defeat:
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 3, player 2, area (40,60)-(55,75) [path "Defeat - City Falls"]
issues_found: No Janissaries: the Ottoman storming force consists entirely of Camel Riders, Cavalry Archers and Light Cavalry plus artillery, yet the Janissary is in the editor's Turkish roster and was the actual assault infantry at the Carinthian Gate. Cavalry charging a walled breach is historically backwards.

The Ottoman side has no infantry at all and no Villager-type sappers beyond a single VILLAGER_MALE, so the mining/countermining that the narration makes central is represented by one unit against a force of horsemen.

'Spanish arquebusiers' are rendered as CROSSBOWMAN x8 when the editor offers Hand Cannoneers (and Turkish/Teutonic gunpowder units) — an avoidable substitution given the text explicitly names firearms.

Garrison strength is token (1 Champion, 8 Pikemen, 8 Crossbowmen, 4 Spearmen) for a defence of roughly 17-20,000 men behind Vienna's walls; the wall circuit (192 stone wall segments) is far better represented than the men on it.
Salm is said to be wounded on 11 October; he was struck by stone splinters during the final assault of 14 October.
ONAGER x2 alongside MANGONEL x3 is an odd choice for 1529 — the Ottoman siege was dominated by cannon and mines, and only 2 Bombard Cannon are placed.
The 300-second victory timer compresses three dated assaults, a mine, and the autumn rains into five minutes, making the 'hold out' far shorter than the three-week hold the brief describes.
strengths: Correct civilizations explicitly assigned: Teutons for the German/Imperial garrison of Vienna, Turks for Suleiman's army.
Suleiman is a renamed generic KING and Salm a renamed CHAMPION — the correct handling where the engine ships no hero for either figure.
The Ottoman camp is built as tents (TENT_D/E x12), a PAVILION_C for the Sultan, bonfire and flag, matching the encamped besieger rather than a permanent town.

Victory is gated on outlasting a deadline and defeat on Ottoman units penetrating the city interior (3 units in the area around 40-55, 60-75) — exactly the shape of a siege the defenders only had to survive.

The mine-and-countermine subplot is modelled with real branching: killing the sapper preserves the wall, while BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA blows a breach and spawns attackers, which is the defining tactical feature of this siege.

Dated assault waves (29 September, 6 October, 11 October) and the 14 October withdrawal driven by rain and supply failure follow the actual chronology and outcome without inventing a battlefield victory.
justification: The scenario gets the sides, the walls, and the shape of the siege right: Teutons behind 192 wall segments and a named gate, Turks in a tent camp with cannon, a countermine subplot that branches on whether the sapper reaches the wall, and a timer-plus-breakthrough win/loss pair that correctly encodes 'outlast the besieger'. The chief avoidable fault is the Ottoman order of battle: no Janissaries and no infantry whatsoever, so the assaults on the Carinthian Gate are delivered by Camel Riders and Light Cavalry, and the text's 'Spanish arquebusiers' appear as Crossbowmen despite gunpowder units being available in the editor. The 300-second victory timer is long enough for the scripted sequence to run but reduces a three-week hold to five minutes, and Salm's wounding is moved from 14 to 11 October.

issues_found: The garrison is described as 'Landsknechts and Spanish arquebusiers' but the placed defenders are 8 Crossbowmen; the Teutons have access to Hand Cannoneers, which would have represented the arquebusiers, so the gunpowder-infantry element of the defence is avoidably absent.

'29 September: The first great assault' is invented/misdated — the Ottomans had only just completed their investment around 27 September, and the serious assaults on the breaches fell between 9 and 14 October.
Salm is shown wounded on 11 October; he was in fact struck by stone splinters during the final great assault of 14 October.

Onagers and Mangonels appear alongside Bombard Cannons; the Ottoman siege train at Vienna was notoriously light in heavy guns (the big pieces were lost in the mud), and torsion artillery is an anachronistic addition for 1529 when bombards alone would have sufficed.
The victory timer of 300 seconds compresses the whole three-week siege into five minutes, making the 'hold until the rains' framing very thin as a test of endurance.
strengths: Correct opposing civilisations: Teutons for the Viennese/Imperial garrison and Turks for the Ottomans, with Turkish tents, pavilion, bonfire and flag forming a recognisable siege camp outside the walls.
192 Stone Wall segments plus a named Gate, Keep and Guard Towers give a genuine fortified city rather than an open-field fight.

The countermining episode — the historically decisive feature of the 1529 siege — is modelled as a named Sapper that must be destroyed before reaching the Carinthian Gate, with a branch that opens a breach if he arrives.
Pikemen for Landsknecht pike blocks is an apt engine abstraction.
The outcome is correct: no counter-offensive is required, and the Ottomans withdraw on 14 October because of rain and exhausted supplies, exactly as the sources report.

Victory is gated on outlasting the siege (a timer) rather than on destroying the besieging army, which is the right form for this engagement, and the defeat condition — Ottoman troops penetrating the city centre area — can fire first.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right: Teutons behind 192 tiles of stone wall against a Turkish camp, victory by outlasting rather than by killing Suleiman, defeat if Ottoman troops reach the city's heart, and the countermining duel over the Carinthian Gate reproduced as a named Sapper race. The forces, however, are avoidably wrong in detail — the 'Spanish arquebusiers' of the narration are actually Crossbowmen when Teutonic Hand Cannoneers were available, and the Ottoman storming parties consist entirely of camels, light cavalry and horse archers with not one Janissary, despite the Turkish roster shipping them. Dates drift as well: a 'first great assault' on 29 September and Salm's wounding on 11 October both precede their real occurrences, though the 14 October withdrawal for rain and failing supplies is sound. The five-minute victory timer is a real hold that the defeat condition can pre-empt, but it compresses three weeks very hard.

title: The Siege of Vienna
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from

Victory:

Defeat:

issues_found: The Ottoman assault force contains no infantry at all: CAMEL_RIDER x6, CAVALRY_ARCHER x6 and LIGHT_CAVALRY x4 carry the attacks on the Carinthian Gate, yet the Turks in this engine ship the JANISSARY, the very unit that led the historical storming parties. This is an avoidable substitution and the camel riders are wholly out of place before Vienna.

Suleiman is represented by a KING, a non-combat pageant unit; a renamed Elite Janissary or Cavalry Archer would have been a defensible stand-in for a sultan who was present with the army, and the King cannot participate in the siege in any way.

The 'Spanish arquebusiers' named in Salm's speech are placed as CROSSBOWMAN x8 — a firearms garrison rendered as bowmen when Teuton gunpowder infantry (Hand Cannoneer) was available; the placed content contradicts the text.

The Landsknecht core of the garrison is represented by PIKEMAN x8 and SPEARMAN x4 with a single CHAMPION; two-handed swordsmen or more Champions would better match a body of doppelsoldner, and 21 total defenders is a very thin abstraction of ~20,000.
No Danube or arm of the river anywhere on the map, and 1,414 oak trees dominate the terrain; Vienna's setting was a walled city on a major river with a cleared glacis, not deep woodland.

The first great assault is dated 29 September; the Ottomans had only just closed the investment (27 September) and the serious mine-and-assault phase belongs to 6-14 October. Salm's wounding is placed on 11 October rather than during the final assault of 14 October.
Victory at 300 seconds compresses three dated assaults, a countermine sequence and the onset of the rains into five minutes, which is a thin 'hold' for a three-week siege.
strengths: Correct opposed civilizations explicitly assigned: TEUTONS for the Vienna garrison (Central European architecture, stone walls, keep) against TURKS for Suleiman's army.
The Ottoman siege train is right in kind: BOMBARD_CANNON x2, MANGONEL x3, ONAGER x2 and a SIEGE_WORKSHOP, with a besiegers' camp of TENT_D/TENT_E x12, PAVILION_C, FLAG_D and a BONFIRE.
192 STONE_WALL segments plus a named GATE_NORTH_TO_SOUTH give the scenario an actual medieval circuit and a specific Carinthian Gate to fight over, as the sources single out.

The mine war is modelled rather than narrated: a renamed VILLAGER_MALE sapper with distinct Countermine Success (DESTROY_OBJECT) and Countermine Failure (BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA, which breaches and spawns attackers) branches.
Salm and Suleiman are both cast via CHANGE_OBJECT_NAME on placed units rather than being absent or replaced by an unrelated engine hero.

Victory is a survival timer and defeat fires when 3 Player 2 objects reach the city centre area (40,60)-(55,75) — the correct shape for a siege the defenders had only to outlast, with a genuine losing condition available throughout.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right — Teutons behind 192 wall tiles and a named Carinthian Gate against a Turkish camp with bombard cannon, mangonels and a tented siege park, with Salm and Suleiman cast onto placed units and a real countermine branch that either kills the sapper or blows a breach. The chief avoidable fault is the assault force: the Ottomans attack with camel riders, light cavalry and cavalry archers when the Turks in this engine field Janissaries, and the 'Spanish arquebusiers' of the narration appear as crossbowmen, so the placed units contradict the text on both sides. The encoded goal is the correct kind — outlast the besieger on a timer while a breach into the city centre can lose it — though 300 seconds compresses the 29 September, 6 October and 11 October assaults into a very brief hold, and the 29 September date is itself invented. Narration otherwise tracks the sources closely, including the mines, the rains, the exhausted supplies and the 14 October withdrawal.
